items.stem: The review notes that "hippie" became a political insult and campuses became battlegrounds in the late 1960s. What does that development show?
options: (A) Most ordinary Americans became hippies themselves
(B) Colleges closed their doors for the rest of the decade
(C) The cultural split had become a political weapon
(D) Nixon publicly supported the counterculture's goals
items.explanation: Turning "hippie" into an insult and campuses into battlegrounds meant the cultural divide was being used as a tool of politics, mobilizing the backlash.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The insult worked because most Americans were not hippies and disapproved of them.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Campuses stayed open; "battlegrounds" describes political conflict, not closure.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The language of cultural contempt became a way to win political support.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Nixon appealed to the opponents of the counterculture, not its supporters.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — the cultural split became a political weapon: "hippie" as an insult, campuses as battlegrounds

items.stem: The review concludes that the culture wars the 1960s counterculture started are still being fought. What does that claim imply about the decade?
options: (A) The counterculture won every political battle that it fought
(B) Young people stopped all protesting after 1969
(C) The "silent majority" disappeared entirely from politics in the 1970s
(D) The cultural divisions of the 1960s outlasted the decade
items.explanation: If the culture wars are still being fought, then the 1960s created political divisions durable enough to structure politics long after the decade ended.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review describes a backlash that defeated much of the counterculture politically.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Protest continued; the point is about the durability of the divisions, not the end of protest.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The silent-majority backlash became a lasting coalition, not a vanished one.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The claim is about continuity: 1960s divisions became long-term political fault lines.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 Youth culture and counterculture — the culture wars it started are still being fought

items.stem: In 1962 Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, documenting how the pesticide DDT was poisoning ecosystems and the people exposed to it. What did the book change in American attitudes?
options: (A) It turned postwar faith in chemical progress into suspicion
(B) It ended all pesticide use in the United States immediately
(C) It convinced Congress to create the EPA that same year
(D) It reassured the public that pesticides were safe
items.explanation: Carson's documentation made readers doubt the postwar assumption that chemical products were pure progress, creating the suspicion that fueled the environmental movement.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The review identifies this reversal — from faith to suspicion — as the book's central effect.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Pesticide use continued; the book changed attitudes, not law, in 1962.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The EPA was created in 1970, eight years later.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The book did the opposite: it alarmed readers about chemical harm.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) documented how the pesticide DDT was poisoning ecosystems and readers, turning postwar faith in chemical progress into suspicion

items.stem: The Santa Barbara oil spill (1969), the Cuyahoga River catching fire, and the Love Canal toxic-waste scandal (1978) all became famous episodes of the environmental era. Why did such disasters matter politically?
options: (A) They were the first pollution events in American history
(B) They made pollution visible, building public demand for action
(C) They convinced industry to regulate itself without new laws
(D) They occurred far from any populated areas
items.explanation: Abstract warnings became undeniable when oil coated beaches, a river burned, and a neighborhood sat on toxic waste — visible disasters converted concern into political pressure.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Pollution long predated these events; their power was visibility, not novelty.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Seeing the damage made the issue concrete for millions of Americans.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The disasters led to demands for federal laws, not trust in self-regulation.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Santa Barbara's beaches, an Ohio river, and a Niagara Falls neighborhood were all populated places.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — a string of visible disasters did the rest: the Santa Barbara oil spill (1969), the Cuyahoga River catching fire, and the Love Canal toxic-waste scandal (1978)

items.stem: On April 22, 1970, some 20 million Americans joined the first Earth Day. What did that turnout demonstrate?
options: (A) Most Americans went to work for the newly created EPA
(B) Congress opposed all environmental legislation that year
(C) Environmental concern was a mass cause
(D) The movement was confined to the state of California
items.explanation: Twenty million participants proved environmental concern reached far beyond activists, which is why Congress answered with the decade's major statutes.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The EPA was created in 1970, but participants were ordinary citizens, not agency employees.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Congress responded to Earth Day by passing environmental laws.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The scale of participation showed the cause had mass support.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Earth Day was a national event, not a California one.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — on April 22, 1970, some 20 million Americans joined the first Earth Day, and Congress responded with the decade's great environmental statutes

items.stem: The review says environmentalism used the same tools as the civil rights movement: moral claims, media events, and federal legislation. Which of the following best shows that shared toolkit in action?
options: (A) Earth Day's moral appeal and media event, followed by federal legislation
(B) State environmental laws combined with voluntary industry codes of conduct
(C) Federal court orders backed by military enforcement power
(D) International environmental treaties negotiated with foreign governments abroad
items.explanation: Earth Day supplied the moral claim and the media event; the wave of federal statutes supplied the legislation — the same three-part pattern the civil rights movement had used.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Mass mobilization plus moral argument produced federal legislation, the civil-rights pattern.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The movement's victories were federal statutes, not state laws and voluntary codes.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. That describes school desegregation enforcement, not the environmental movement's method.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The movement's landmark wins were domestic federal laws, not treaties.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — it used the same tools as civil rights (moral claims, media events, federal legislation): the EPA (1970), Clean Air Act (1970), Clean Water Act (1972), Endangered Species Act (1973)

items.stem: A student is matching the decade's environmental laws to their years. Which match is correct?
options: (A) Clean Water Act — 1970
(B) Clean Air Act — 1970
(C) Endangered Species Act — 1970
(D) EPA created — 1972
items.explanation: The Clean Air Act passed in 1970; the EPA was also created in 1970, while the Clean Water Act came in 1972 and the Endangered Species Act in 1973.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Clean Water Act was 1972, not 1970.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Clean Air Act is the 1970 statute in this set.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Endangered Species Act was 1973, not 1970.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The EPA was created in 1970, not 1972.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — the Environmental Protection Agency (created 1970), the Clean Air Act (1970), the Clean Water Act (1972), and the Endangered Species Act (1973)

items.stem: A historian claims the 1979 Three Mile Island accident proves nuclear power released deadly radiation across Pennsylvania. What is wrong with this claim?

stimulus.text: The 1979 Three Mile Island nuclear accident in Pennsylvania terrified the public and effectively froze new nuclear plant construction — even though almost no radiation escaped.

options: (A) No accident ever happened at Three Mile Island
(B) Almost no radiation escaped; public fear froze construction
(C) The frightened public demanded more nuclear plants after the accident
(D) Three Mile Island was actually a chemical plant, not a nuclear one
items.explanation: The evidence supports a claim about perception, not about measured harm: the freeze on construction followed terror, while the radiation release was minimal.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The accident did happen in 1979.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The claim confuses the public's fear with the physical facts, which showed almost no radiation escaped.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The accident froze new construction; it did not increase demand for plants.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Three Mile Island was a nuclear power plant.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — the 1979 Three Mile Island nuclear accident in Pennsylvania terrified the public and effectively froze new nuclear plant construction, even though almost no radiation escaped

items.stem: In the West, ranchers and miners launched the Sagebrush Rebellion, demanding that federal lands be turned over to the states. What drove them?
options: (A) Their support for the Endangered Species Act
(B) Opposition to continued American involvement in the Vietnam War
(C) A demand for more federal regulation of mining
(D) Federal regulation threatened their jobs and livelihoods
items.explanation: The rebellion was the western expression of the anti-regulation backlash: people whose work depended on federal lands saw regulation as a threat to their livelihoods.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The rebellion opposed the regulatory regime the Act represented.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The rebellion was about land and regulation, not the war.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The rebels wanted less federal control, not more.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Economic self-interest — jobs and livelihoods — drove the demand for state control of the lands.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — in the West, ranchers and miners launched the Sagebrush Rebellion, demanding federal lands be turned over to the states; a conservative backlash arguing that regulation threatened jobs and freedom

items.stem: The review says environmentalism "hit the same wall" as the civil rights movement: a conservative backlash arguing that federal action threatened jobs and freedom. What does "the same wall" mean?
options: (A) Both movements failed to pass any significant federal laws at all
(B) Both movements were led by exactly the same national leaders
(C) Both movements' reforms provoked organized conservative opposition
(D) Both movements opposed the creation of the EPA in 1970
items.explanation: The "wall" is the pattern: ambitious federal reform triggers an organized backlash arguing Washington threatens livelihoods and liberty — and it stopped further advance in both cases.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Both movements passed landmark federal laws; the wall came after the victories.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The parallel is in the political dynamic, not the personnel.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The same backlash argument — jobs and freedom — met both movements' federal programs.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The EPA was environmentalism's own creation, not something civil rights opposed.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — it used the same tools as civil rights (moral claims, media events, federal legislation) and hit the same wall: a conservative backlash arguing that regulation threatened jobs and freedom
